sentences.text: Net interest income compounded from $46.1 billion in FY2016 [F1] to $95.4 billion in FY2025 [F10], an 8.4% CAGR [F111].
Net income was $24.7 billion in FY2016 [F21] and $57.0 billion in FY2025 [F30], with falls of 20.0% in FY2020 [D94] and 21.9% in FY2022 [D142].
Net interest income jumped 33.8% to $89.3 billion in FY2023 [D174][F8], which the 10-K attributes to higher rates [P36].
Net interest income fell 4.7% in FY2020 [D100], a move the business-level discussion ties to deposit margin compression [P67].
Net interest income compounded 8.4% [F111] against 6.2% [F112] for noninterest income, lifting its revenue share from 47.7% [D8] to 52.3% [D209].
In FY2025 net interest income rose 3.1% to $95.4 billion [D221][F10], driven by higher Markets net interest income and Card revolving balances [P28].
Noninterest income rose 2.4% to $87.0 billion [D222][F20] on Markets and asset-management fees, offset by the absence of a $7.9 billion Visa gain [P27].
CIB noninterest revenue rose to $53.8 billion from $48.3 billion [S134][S133].
Diluted EPS rose 1.4% [D216] as diluted shares fell 3.4% [D224], although 10-K net income fell from $58.5 billion [X19] to $57.0 billion [X20].
The FY2025 efficiency ratio of 52.4% [D207] is below the window median of 57.2% [D333] and the 61.7% peer median [D337].
Net margin of 31.2% [D210] sits between the window low of 24.3% [D18] and high of 39.7% [D114].
Noninterest expense rose 4.2% [D225] to $95.6 billion [X137], driven by compensation and brokerage costs, partly offset by FDIC accrual releases [P26].
The largest move was FY2021's net margin rise from 24.3% in FY2020 [D90] to 39.7% [D114], as the provision fell from 14.6% [D88] to -7.6% of revenue [D112] on improved credit [P55].
The effective tax rate rose to 21.4% [D203] from 17.7% [D83] in FY2020, and the cited passages do not explain it.
Operating cash flow was -$147.8 billion in FY2025 [F60] against net income of $57.0 billion [F30], a ratio of -2.59x [D204].
The outflow reflected higher trading assets and securities borrowed, partly offset by net income [P21].
For a bank, operating cash flow is not a meaningful earnings-quality measure, so capital return against net income is the better test.
Capex is not in the pack, so capital intensity cannot be measured; depreciation and amortization was $8.82 billion [X40].
Loans were 57.3% of deposits in FY2025 [D211], down from 64.7% in FY2016 [D10]; net cash does not apply to a bank.
Loans rose $121 billion in FY2025, predominantly in CIB Markets [P4].
Return on average equity of 16.1% [D213] ranks at the 100th percentile among seven banks [D338], against an 11.8% peer median [D339].
Diluted shares fell 3.4% [D224] in FY2025, alongside buybacks of $31.6 billion [X102] and dividends of $16.6 billion [X112].
Credit-loss provisions have risen three straight years, from $6.39 billion in FY2022 [X144] to $14.2 billion in FY2025 [X147].

At 7.8% of revenue [D208] the provision is above the 6.0% peer median [D341], ranking 75th percentile of four banks [D340]; the stated cause is wholesale: criticized exposure rose to $48.5 billion from $44.7 billion, driven by downgrades in SPEs and Consumer & Retail [P2].
Net income for FY2021 to FY2025 is proxy-sourced [R1], so FY2021 growth of 65.8% [D118] is approximate; the 10-K figure is $48.3 billion [X16].
A fall back toward FY2016's 5.6% [D7] would reverse the trend; a rise above 7.8% [D208] would confirm it in the FY2026 10-K.
An efficiency ratio above 52.4% [D207] would confirm costs outrunning revenue; a return below the 51.7% window low [D331] would show leverage recovering, in the FY2026 10-K.
Criticized exposure above $48.5 billion [P2] in the FY2026 10-K would confirm the wholesale credit deterioration behind the provision rise.
